items.prompt: Users open a home timeline 20 times for every post they write, the average account has 200 followers, and the timeline must load in under 200 ms. When should the timeline be built?
items.why: One write has many recipients and reads dominate → fan-out on write: precompute each follower's timeline when the post is made so a read is one lookup.

items.prompt: Push-based timelines work well, except when an account with 60 million followers posts: its followers see the post 10 minutes late and the workers lag for everyone.
items.why: A skewed fan-out degree is the cue for the hybrid: don't push for accounts above a follower threshold, merge their posts in at read time.

items.prompt: The post service must not wait while thousands of follower timelines are updated; the work should be retried if a worker crashes halfway.
items.why: The question is about the transport: hand the post event to a durable queue or log so the fan-out runs asynchronously with retries. Fan-out already decided that copies are made.

items.prompt: A chat app must show a new message on a recipient's open screen within 200 ms, without the phone polling.
items.why: Getting a message onto an online client over a long-lived connection (WebSocket/SSE) is the delivery hop, not the choice of when to make per-recipient copies.

items.prompt: A message to a 150-member group must land in every member's inbox so each can read their history on any device.
items.why: One message, a bounded set of recipients, each with their own inbox → fan-out on write to every member, done by async workers.

items.prompt: The recent posts of the 1 000 biggest accounts are read on almost every feed open and the cache node holding them is saturated.
items.why: The fan-out choice is already made (pull for big accounts); the issue is a few keys taking a huge share of reads → replicate those hot keys across cache nodes.

items.prompt: Each user's home page is ranked by an ML model using live signals at the moment they open it; results can't be computed in advance.
items.why: Results that depend on read time are an anti-signal for push. Query the candidate sources in parallel at read time and merge them.

items.prompt: When a creator finishes uploading a video, it must be split into 2 000 segment × resolution jobs processed in parallel by many workers.
items.why: One event turned into many independent units of work is fan-out on write (jobs created at upload time), with a queue carrying them to workers.
